title: SE-GA: Memory-Augmented Self-Evolution for GUI Agents
one_liner: SE-GA helps a GUI agent finish long screen tasks by retrieving the right past experience at each step and then turning those solved runs into better future behavior.
lead: A GUI agent often fails for a simple reason: the next click depends on facts that appeared many screens earlier, but the agent only has a short working view of the task. SE-GA tackles that gap with a memory system that brings back the most useful past experience when the agent is deciding what to do on the current screen. It then uses solved runs to improve later runs, because the agent should keep more of what worked and less of what failed.

problem.h2: Why long GUI tasks break ordinary agents
paras: A long GUI task spreads its evidence across many moments. The task goal may appear in the first instruction, the needed setting may appear halfway through, and the final confirmation may depend on both. A plain agent often drops one of those pieces because its working view is short and because each new screen pushes older details out of view.

That weakness becomes worse when the task branches. The agent may have solved a similar screen before, but if it cannot recover that past run at the right time, it starts the reasoning from scratch. SE-GA treats this as a memory problem first, because better retrieval can restore the missing facts before the next action is chosen.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence.
callout.html: Store task experience in several memory banks, retrieve the parts that match the current screen, and recycle successful runs into future training so that the agent keeps improving from its own work.

panels.title: 1. A long task starts
panels.viz_args: instruction -> several app screens -> final goal
panels.caption: The agent must carry important facts across many screens because the task cannot be finished from the current screen alone.

panels.title: 2. Useful past runs exist
panels.caption: Past runs hold clues about what to click next, which field matters, and which order avoids dead ends.

panels.title: 3. Retrieval happens at decision time
panels.viz_args: current screen + goal -> fetch matching memories
panels.caption: The agent asks for past experience that matches the current screen and task goal so that it gets relevant context instead of raw history.

panels.title: 4. The next action improves
panels.viz_args: screen facts + recalled steps -> choose action
panels.caption: The next action is better because the agent now sees both the current screen and the past evidence that matters for it.

panels.title: 5. Solved runs go back into memory
panels.caption: A successful run becomes new material for later tasks, so the agent's usable experience grows over time.

steps.text: Read the current screen, the task goal, and the recent action history so that the agent knows where it is.
Retrieve matching past screens, task facts, and solved runs because each bank stores a different kind of useful evidence.

steps.b: Step 3: Build an enriched working view
steps.text: Combine the current screen with the recalled items so that older but still relevant facts are visible again.
Choose the next click, type action, or scroll based on that enriched view.
Keep data from strong runs and use it to improve later behavior, because repeated good solutions should shape the agent's future choices.

paras: The paper changes the agent's working state. Instead of forcing every decision to depend only on a short recent history, it adds retrieved long-range task evidence and then loops solved runs back into training.

hidden.name: how much of the task-relevant past is present when the agent chooses the next action
paras: The most important quantity is decision-time coverage. The agent may have seen the needed evidence earlier, but the real question is whether that evidence is present when the current action is chosen.

SE-GA raises coverage by storing different forms of past experience and then retrieving the pieces that fit the current screen. That matters because a long task fails when the missing fact is absent at the exact decision point, not because the fact was never seen at all.

heat.caption: Dark cells mark pieces of past evidence that become available at the moment of action selection.

reads.html: The system wins when the agent has the right old clue in front of it before it clicks.
SE-GA improves long-horizon GUI control by retrieving episodic, semantic, and experiential memory at decision time so that more task-relevant evidence survives across many screens.

paras: The memory split matters because not all useful past information has the same form. One part is a remembered screen and what happened on it. Another part is a short rule about the task. Another part is a higher-level solved run. Keeping those apart helps retrieval because each memory bank can answer a different question.

The self-evolution step matters because retrieval alone only helps the current run. When the system turns strong runs into new training material, the base agent itself gets better because later tasks begin with policies that already absorbed those successful patterns.

The paper's gains fit this story because GUI tasks depend heavily on delayed evidence. A retrieval system that restores delayed evidence improves action choice by putting the missing clue back into the working view, and a training loop that keeps the best recovered runs improves future action choice by preserving those successful patterns in the base agent.

stages.s: search screen, rule, and solved-run memory
merge recalled evidence into the working view
save strong runs for later improvement

math.words: Choose the next action using the current screen plus the recalled memories that best match it, then favor training updates from finished runs that solve the task with fewer mistakes.
math.equation: J = E[ success(a_t | s_t, M_t) + alpha * useful_recall(M_t, s_t) - beta * error_steps ]
symbols: the expected objective over GUI episodes
the action chosen at step t
the current screen state and task goal at step t
the memories retrieved for the current step
reward for taking actions that finish the task when current evidence and recalled evidence are both used
how well the retrieved memories match what the current screen needs
wasted actions such as wrong clicks, detours, or repeated corrections

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: The task is to enable a setting that is buried three menus deep.
At the final menu, the current screen alone shows two similar options.
The memory search recalls an earlier solved run saying that the correct option sits under the privacy menu, not the account menu.
The agent clicks the privacy path, reaches the right toggle, and avoids two wrong detours.
That run earns a higher objective because the recalled evidence matched the screen and reduced wasted steps.

math.note: The exact training details are richer than this summary, but this compact form captures the paper's main idea: reward actions that solve the GUI task while rewarding retrieval that brings back the right old evidence.

charts.title: Plain GUI agent without SE-GA
charts.note: A plain agent drops older clues during long tasks, so later actions drift when the screen path is long or changes slightly.

charts.title: SE-GA
charts.note: The paper reports stronger task completion because the agent can recover relevant past evidence at each step and then keep learning from solved runs.

items.html: A bad recall can hurt the current step because it pushes the agent toward a screen that only looked similar on the surface.
If the saved experience is noisy or repetitive, later retrieval becomes less helpful because the best signals are buried under weak ones.
If a flawed run is treated as good training material, later behavior may copy the wrong pattern because the loop keeps feeding that pattern back.

The method works when retrieval ranks the right past evidence highly and the self-evolution stage keeps only runs that solve the task cleanly, because then both the current step and the next round benefit.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small desktop task with six to eight screens and at least one delayed dependency, such as reading a code on the first screen and entering it on the fifth. Run one agent with only the recent history and another with memory retrieval from past solved runs. Then add the self-evolution loop by saving clean solved runs and reusing them in later trials.
The demo should show fewer wasted steps and higher task completion for the memory-augmented agent because the delayed clue is present again at the moment it matters.
demo.metric_eq: task_success = solved_tasks / total_tasks ; wasted_steps = wrong_actions / total_actions ; recall_hit_rate = useful_recalls / total_recalls
demo.closing: The key evidence is that retrieval restores the missing old clue and the self-evolution loop keeps that gain alive in later tasks, because the same successful pattern first repairs the current run and then becomes part of later behavior.
